entities.description: Chicago producer of the 1986 Trax classic 'No Way Back'; the record's specific gear chain is unverified.
entities.chicago_connection: Chicago acid/house producer; 'No Way Back' on Trax (1986)

claims.claim: Adonis (Michael Smith) wrote and produced 'No Way Back' (Trax TX112, 1986); Discogs community notes praise its 'tightest sequenced TR-808' production
claims.evidence: Discogs release page for Adonis 'No Way Back'
claims.uncertainty: No interview or primary source found naming the drum machine or recording chain — gear attribution Unresolved; do not assert TR-808

entities.name: Afrime Studios
entities.description: Black-led independent game studio (founded by Crandon Dillard with Erik Reynolds) building the Afrofuturist Unyverse IP against extreme venture underfunding.

claims.claim: Afrime Studios is a Black-led game studio building 'Unyverse'; founder Crandon Dillard and co-founder Erik Reynolds; Black-led game studios receive roughly 0.04% of venture capital funding
claims.evidence: PocketGamer.biz interview with Dillard and Reynolds about funding Unyverse; 'Black-led game studios receive roughly 0.04% of venture capital funding.'
claims.uncertainty: studio is US-based building Afrofuturist IP; launch status not verified

entities.name: Benjamin Banneker
entities.description: African American surveyor, astronomer, and almanac author (1731-1806). Circulated clock claim graded: Exaggerated. Banneker did build a working all-wooden striking clock ~1753 by studying a borrowed pocket watch — extraordinary for a self-taught 22-year-old. He did not invent the clock, and his was not the first A

myth_audit.claim_as_circulated: Benjamin Banneker invented the clock / built the first clock in America.
myth_audit.what_is_documented: Banneker did build a working all-wooden striking clock ~1753 by studying a borrowed pocket watch — extraordinary for a self-taught 22-year-old. He did not invent the clock, and his was not the first American-made clock; colonial clockmakers had worked for over a century. His documented scientific achievements are the almanacs and astronomical predictions.
myth_audit.myth_origin: 19th- and 20th-century biographical inflation: a genuine reverse-engineering achievement was retold as 'invented the clock' and then 'first clock in America,' a claim refuted by horological scholarship (Bedini, 1972).

entities.name: Bessie Blount Griffin
entities.description: Bessie Blount Griffin received US 2,550,554 on 1951-04-24 for a 'Portable Receptacle Support' (a neck-worn support holding a bowl or cup for self-feeding by patients unable to use their arms).

claims.claim: Bessie Blount Griffin received US 2,550,554 on 1951-04-24 for a 'Portable Receptacle Support' (a neck-worn support holding a bowl or cup for self-feeding by patients unable to use their arms).
claims.evidence: Smithsonian Magazine (2018-02) quotes the USPTO record directly: 'Portable Receptacle Support,' B.V. Griffin, April 24, 1951, U.S. Pat. No. 2,550,554; National Business League corroborates the 1951 patent.
claims.uncertainty: None material; the USPTO citation is quoted verbatim in the source.

claims.claim: Blount, a nurse and physical therapist, developed an electric self-feeding apparatus for amputee veterans around 1948; after the Veterans Administration rejected it as 'impractical' (letter from chief director Paul B. Magnuson), she granted the rights to the French government for use in military hospitals (1952) without payment.
claims.evidence: Smithsonian Magazine profile documents the five-year development, the VA rejection letter, and the 1952 French arrangement; Face2Face Africa corroborates the French licensing.
claims.uncertainty: Whether the electric apparatus itself was separately patented is unclear; the 1951 patent covers the portable receptacle support.

claims.claim: Blount later became a forensic handwriting/document examiner, trained at Scotland Yard in the 1970s, and was widely recognized as the first Black woman to receive advanced forensic training there.
claims.evidence: National Business League and Face2Face Africa profiles document the Scotland Yard training and forensic career.
claims.uncertainty: 'First Black woman' framing comes from secondary sources; institutional confirmation not captured in this session.

entities.name: Bill Putnam
entities.description: Founder of Universal Recording in Chicago; the studio's technical advances and his mentorship of engineers shaped the sound of Chicago blues recording.
entities.chicago_connection: Founded Universal Recording in Chicago (1946; 46 E. Walton St. from 1955); mentor to Malcolm Chisholm; Chess cut early sides at Universal before 2120 opened

claims.claim: Bill Putnam founded Universal Recording, Chicago's largest independent recording studio; under Putnam the studio pioneered tape repeat, the vocal booth, multiple-voice recording, early 8-track use, studio delay lines, and half-speed-mastered discs (Mercury, 1956)
claims.evidence: Wikipedia 'Universal Recording Corporation'
claims.uncertainty: Tertiary summary; 'firsts' claims need primary/period verification

claims.claim: Malcolm Chisholm 'entered the recording industry under Bill Putnam (1920–1989) at Universal Recording'
claims.evidence: Linden (2013), MEIEA Journal

entities.name: Black assembly workers at Ford Chicago Assembly Plant
entities.description: Black hourly workers at Ford's Torrence Avenue (Hegewisch) assembly plant — the company's oldest continuously operated plant — operating stamping presses, assembly lines, and modern robotic/flexible-manufacturing systems.
entities.chicago_connection: Plant at E. 130th St. and Torrence Ave., Hegewisch, Chicago; opened 1924 for Model T production; ~5,800 hourly workers; UAW Locals 551 and 588.

claims.claim: Chicago Assembly opened March 3, 1924 as an alternative to River Rouge for Model T production; it is Ford's oldest continuously operated plant and a center for flexible just-in-time production employing about 5,800 workers, mostly hourly.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (Chicago Assembly Plant): 'Production started on March 3, 1924, as an alternative site to the River Rouge Plant for Model T production... Ford's Chicago plant is a center for flexible just-in-time production... employed about 5,800 workers, mostly paid per hour.'
claims.uncertainty: Secondary synthesis; headcount and production claims not verified against Ford filings.

claims.claim: A large share of the Chicago plants' blue-collar workforce is Black — reporting on the plants' harassment cases describes the affected women workers as 'female, blue-collar, and black — as so many of them are.'
claims.evidence: Ford Authority (summarizing NYT reporting, 2017): 'being female, blue-collar, and black - as so many of them are - can be risk factors for being left out of social justice movements.' EEOC settlements: $7.75M (1999) and up to $10.125M (2017) over sexual/racial harassment at the Chicago Assembly and Stamping plants.
claims.source: Ford Authority (2017); theautowire (2026, on EEOC settlements)
claims.uncertainty: Evidence establishes substantial Black workforce presence, not specific operator-technology assignments; the record is filtered through harassment litigation.

entities.name: Black brakemen, switchmen, and conductors working under porter title
entities.description: Black railroad workers who performed skilled operating-craft work (braking, switching, conductor duties) but were retained under the title and pay of 'porter.'
entities.chicago_connection: Employed on trains operating through Chicago's Pullman and mainline terminals; Chicago was the Pullman Company's headquarters city.

claims.claim: Some porters worked as brakemen, conductors, and switchmen — skilled jobs traditionally held by white railroad workers — but were still titled and paid as porters.
claims.evidence: Black Enterprise: 'The responsibilities of porters extended beyond serving passengers, with some porters working as brakemen, conductors, and switchmen–skilled jobs traditionally held by white railroad workers — but blacks were still given the title of porter and were paid substantially less.'
claims.source: Black Enterprise, 'Pullman Porters: Ambassadors of Railroad's Golden Era'
claims.uncertainty: Single journalism source quoting historian Hughes; no named individuals or primary payroll records located.

claims.claim: White Pullman conductors were 'invariably white' while porters were Black, formalizing the racial division of operating authority on the car.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'Porters worked under the supervision of a Pullman conductor (distinct from the railroad's own conductor in overall charge of the train), who was invariably white.'
claims.uncertainty: Secondary synthesis; consistent with other accounts.

entities.name: Black Chicago packinghouse killing-floor workers
entities.description: Black workers — many Great Migration migrants from the South — employed on the killing floors and in the processing departments of Chicago's Union Stock Yards meatpacking plants.
entities.chicago_connection: Chicago Union Stock Yards (Packingtown); workers lived in Bronzeville/Black Belt; 1919 Chicago race riot centered in part on the Yards; plants of the major packers on Chicago's South Side.

claims.claim: By the mid-1930s, killing floors showed 'a large representation of black workers' alongside Polish and Lithuanian workers; African-Americans were 'seldom... within the mechanical trades.'
claims.evidence: 'The Chicago stockyards on the eve of the CIO (1936)': 'Concentrations of certain ethnic groups tended to be found in particular departments and occupations. Polish and Lithuanians might be dominant on a killing floor with a large representation of black workers... Seldom were African-Americans within the mechanical trades.'
claims.source: 'The Chicago stockyards on the eve of the CIO (1936)' (scholarly essay via thefreelibrary)
claims.uncertainty: Secondary reprint of a scholarly essay; department-level staffing inferred from period observation.

claims.claim: Racist personnel policies funneled Black workers to the onerous and dangerous killing-floor jobs, which made them indispensable to production: 'without them the whole process would have stalled.'
claims.evidence: Review of Rick Halpern, Meatpackers: An Oral History of Black Packinghouse Workers (thefreelibrary): 'those very same jobs provided a modicum of security... the racist personnel policies that funneled black workers to the onerous and dangerous jobs on the "killing floor" actually made black workers indispensable to production, since without them the whole process would have stalled.'
claims.source: Review of Halpern, Meatpackers: An Oral History of Black Packinghouse Workers and Their Struggle for Racial and Economic Equality (thefreelibrary)
claims.uncertainty: Summary of oral-history findings via a book review, not the oral histories themselves.

claims.claim: After the 1919 Chicago race riot, packing companies arranged for state militia to escort Black workers into the yards; union leaders warned, 'These men will be on the killing floor of the packing plants. They will have cleavers and knives. They know how to use them.'
claims.evidence: Rick Halpern, 'Race, Ethnicity, and Union in the Chicago Stockyards, 1917-1922' (Cambridge): '"These men will be on the killing floor of the packing plants. They will have cleavers and knives. They know how to use them."'
claims.uncertainty: Quoted union testimony from the 1919 crisis; documents both the tools operated and the skill ascribed to Black killing-floor workers.

claims.claim: Chicago packing plants ran on overhead drag lines, conveyor belts, and automated disassembly systems; a company management manual stated 'There is no room for individuality or artistry in beef butchering. The worker does not decide where or how to make his cut.'
claims.evidence: Current Affairs (2025): 'The overhead drag lines, conveyor belts, and automated systems that disciplined animals into profitable submission... A management manual from a Chicago packing plant explained the philosophy.'
claims.source: Current Affairs, 'How Industrial Slaughter Became the Blueprint for Modern Capitalism' (2025)
claims.uncertainty: Essayistic synthesis; the manual quotation is attributed but not footnoted in the excerpt.

entities.name: Black Girl Gamers
entities.description: Online community amplifying Black women in gaming through Twitch, YouTube and Facebook; an example of Black gaming community-building outside commercial platforms.

claims.claim: Black Girl Gamers is a London-based community of 6,000+ members amplifying the voices of Black women in gaming through Twitch streams, a YouTube channel and a Facebook group
claims.evidence: Kotaku (2020): 'With more than 6,000 members, the London-based Black Girl Gamers seeks to amplify the voices of black women in gaming through Twitch streams, a YouTube channel, and a Facebook group.'
claims.uncertainty: founders and founding date not verified this pass

entities.name: Black IBEW electricians in Chicago
entities.description: Black journeyman electricians in Chicago who organized a separate IBEW charter in the 1930s and won full membership in Local 134 by 1942, wiring the city's commercial and infrastructure electrical systems.
entities.chicago_connection: Chicago IBEW Local 134; Dunbar High School partnership noted in the Congressional Record (2018) as continuing the pipeline effort.

claims.claim: A 1960 NAACP report found 'almost total exclusion' of Black workers from apprenticeship programs: 60 of 9,360 electrician apprentices (under 1%) were Black; in 1950 only 1% of U.S. electricians were Black.
claims.evidence: ENR: 'A 1960 report by the NAACP was especially damning, citing an "almost total exclusion" of Black workers from apprenticeship programs... 60 of 9,360 electrician apprentices'; reason.com: 'in 1950, only 1 percent of the electricians... in the United States were black.'
claims.source: ENR, 'From the Archives: The Fight to Racially Integrate the US Construction Industry'; reason.com, 'Exclusionary Rule' (1991)
claims.uncertainty: Two independent secondary sources converge on the NAACP figures.

claims.claim: As late as 1961, Black workers were still barred from the unions of electrical workers, operating engineers, plumbers, plasterers, and sheet-metal workers, among others.
claims.evidence: reason.com (1991): 'And as late as 1961, blacks were still barred from the unions of the electrical workers, operating engineers, plumbers, plasterers, and sheet-metal workers, among others.'
claims.uncertainty: Journalistic summary; specific local (e.g., Chicago Local 134) admission dates beyond Taylor Electric's account not verified.

entities.name: Black locomotive firemen and hostlers
entities.description: Black engine-service workers who fired steam locomotives (fueling fireboxes, maintaining boiler water, oiling moving parts) and hostled (moved) locomotives, often for full careers without promotion to engineer.

claims.claim: Many Southern railroads employed Black firemen who worked their whole careers as firemen and could never be promoted to engineer — e.g., a 50-year-old Black fireman paired with a 25-year-old white engineer.
claims.evidence: Trains.com forum discussion of Pullman porters/black railroad labor: 'many southern railroads had black firemen who worked their whole careers as firemen and could never be promoted to engineer, so a 50 year old black fireman might be assigned to work with a 25 year old white engineer.'
claims.uncertainty: Anecdotal forum testimony, not a documented case; pattern is consistent with segregation-era seniority rules.

claims.claim: Black firemen were targets of racial violence: during 1921, five Black firemen on Southern railways were killed and eight injured; between 1931 and 1944, ten died and twenty-one were wounded.
claims.evidence: Common Ground (1946): 'During 1921, five colored firemen on southern railways were killed and eight injured and between 1931 and 1944 ten died and twentyone were wounded.'
claims.uncertainty: Period periodical citing violence statistics; original sourcing of the figures not given in excerpt.

claims.claim: The fireman's job entailed keeping the engine oiled and fueled: steam locomotives had to stop frequently so firemen could jump off with oilcans and lubricate moving parts, preventing overheating and wear.
claims.evidence: Smithsonian via The Engineer (Feb 2024): 'During every run, a locomotive had to make frequent stops for oiling, at which point, the fireman would jump off with an oilcan in hand and lubricate all of the engine's moving parts.'
claims.source: The Engineer, Feb 2024 ('Late Great Engineers,' on Elijah McCoy)
claims.uncertainty: General technical history; corroborates the operator context of firemen like McCoy.

entities.name: Black railroad dining-car cooks and waiters
entities.description: Predominantly Black men who staffed railroad dining cars as cooks and waiters, operating dining-car kitchen and service systems under a (typically white) steward.
entities.chicago_connection: Pullman's first dining car, the Delmonico, ran on the Chicago & Alton between Chicago and Springfield beginning in 1868.

claims.claim: Pullman and railroad dining cars were typically staffed with African-American cooks and waiters under a white steward; a trained staff was required because conductors and porters could no longer do double duty.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (Pullman porter): 'the dining cars were typically staffed with African-American cooks and waiters, under the supervision of a white steward'; NYHistory: Pullman 'hired formerly enslaved men who had worked domestically to be porters, waiters, and cooks.'
claims.uncertainty: Wikipedia cites scholarly sources ([6],[7]); NYHistory is an institutional blog. No company employment roster located.

claims.claim: Charles Johnson became Southern Pacific's first African-American dining car steward after 35+ years of dining-car work; stewards supervised cooks and waiters, collected fares, and filed cash reports with headquarters.
claims.evidence: 'Southern Pacific's first African-American dining car steward' (thefreelibrary): Johnson, born 1912 in Gretna, La., worked 40+ years; 'Stewards supervised the cooks and waiters, greeted and seated passengers, and were responsible for the money received from diners... made reports and turned the money over to the Southern Pacific in San Francisco.' Retired from Amtrak 1979.
claims.source: thefreelibrary, 'Southern Pacific's first African-American dining car steward' (oral-history based)
claims.uncertainty: Oral-history testimony reported in a secondary outlet; promotion date to steward not given in excerpt.

entities.name: Black steelworkers at Inland Steel, Indiana Harbor
entities.description: Black production workers at Inland Steel's Indiana Harbor works who operated furnaces, mills, and finishing equipment while largely excluded from craft and supervisory roles before and during the CIO organizing era.
entities.chicago_connection: Indiana Harbor works in East Chicago, Indiana — part of the Chicago-Calumet steel district; four Inland employees were among those killed in the 1937 Memorial Day Massacre in South Chicago.

claims.claim: During the 1919 steel strike, companies brought 30,000-40,000 unskilled African-American and Mexican American workers into the mills as strikebreakers.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia, '1919 General Steel Strike': 'Between 30,000 and 40,000 unskilled African-American and Mexican American workers were brought to work in the mills.'
claims.uncertainty: Round-number range from a secondary synthesis; company recruiting records not consulted.

claims.claim: In 1980, one in four Black manufacturing workers in Chicago was employed in steel (twice the white rate); 1980s steel losses comprised 40% of all Black manufacturing job losses in the city.
claims.evidence: Parks, 'Revisiting Shibboleths of Race and Urban Economy: Black Employment in Manufacturing and the Public Sector Compared, Chicago 1950-2000' (IJURR, 2011): 'In 1980, one in every four black manufacturing workers was employed in steel, twice as many as whites... steel losses alone comprised 40% of all black manufacturing losses.'
claims.source: Parks, International Journal of Urban and Regional Research (2011), via faculty PDF
claims.uncertainty: Peer-reviewed analysis; documents the depth of Black workers' stake in operating steel technology.

entities.name: Black steelworkers at U.S. Steel Gary Works
entities.description: Black workers recruited during the Great Migration into the Gary, Indiana integrated steelworks — blast furnaces, coke ovens, open-hearth furnaces, rolling mills — mostly confined to unskilled and dangerous jobs.
entities.chicago_connection: Gary Works sits on Lake Michigan at the edge of the Chicago industrial region, integrated with Chicago's factories and rail network; Black workers migrated via Chicago networks.

claims.claim: Gary's Black population grew from 340 (1910) to 5,500 (1920) to 18,000 (1930); mill owners aimed to stabilize Black workers at 10-15% of the workforce as a hedge against class solidarity; Black workers were 'in the main... confined to unskilled jobs.'
claims.evidence: Scholarworks IU (Fort Wayne study, citing Gary steel labor history): 'Gary's black population grew from 340 in 1910 to 5,500 in 1920 and 18,000 in 1930... Gary millowners aimed at stabilizing black workers at around 10 to 15 percent of the work force... Although African Americans in the main were confined to unskilled jobs, the growth of the steel industry in the 1920s sustained the expansion of black employment.'
claims.source: Indiana Magazine of History via scholarworks.iu.edu (scholarly)
claims.uncertainty: Figures are for Gary overall; 10-15% target is an interpretive claim about employer strategy.

claims.claim: Black cranemen operated overhead cranes at Gary Works — equipment so production-critical that when Black cranemen slowed their cranes to protest a discriminatory assignment, 'nothing can operate long without the cranes,' and the whole mill ground to a crawl.
claims.evidence: Anonymous worker memoir 'On the Job in the Nation's Largest Steel Mill: U.S. Steel's Gary Works' (libcom PDF): 'my friend Spider, a black craneman who I often ride to work with... Black cranemen decided to sabotage production until this bullshit was straightened out... They kept the cranes in lowest gear and worked in superslowmotion... Nothing can operate long without the cranes bringing and taking steel, so blacks quietly stopped the whole mill.'
claims.uncertainty: Anonymous firsthand account; individual ('Spider') not independently verified. Demonstrates crane-operation skill and Black workers' presence in a semi-skilled role.

entities.name: Black women in Chicago packinghouse departments
entities.description: Black women employed in the casings, sausage, bacon-packaging, and offal departments of Chicago packing plants — chilled, wet, hazardous departments with piece-rate pay.
entities.chicago_connection: Chicago packinghouses; Black women also attempted to enter Chicago's needle trades when packing work was closed to them.

claims.claim: About 20 percent of a typical plant workforce were women, hired exclusively for jobs requiring dexterity: packaging sliced bacon, preparing casings and linking sausage, packaging lard and smoked meats, cleaning guts.
claims.evidence: 'The Chicago stockyards on the eve of the CIO (1936)': 'About 20 percent of the typical plant workforce were women. They were hired exclusively for certain jobs... such as packaging sliced bacon, preparing casings and linking sausage, packaging lard and smoked meats, or cleaning the guts of the slaughtered animals.'
claims.source: 'The Chicago stockyards on the eve of the CIO (1936)' (thefreelibrary)
claims.uncertainty: General workforce figure; the Black-specific breakdown relies on the following claim.

claims.claim: 'Casings rooms' were among the wettest and most disagreeable places in the plants where 'Black women were found employed in appreciable numbers'; trimmers routinely cut themselves and sometimes lost fingers; cooler/freezer rooms ran 32-40°F.
claims.evidence: Scholarly dissertation text (cdlib mirror): '"Casings rooms", reveals one study of the meat packing industry, "were the wettest and in general, the most disagreeable places in [which] Black women were found employed in appreciable numbers."' Also: 'not uncommon for trimmers in both departments to lose fingers'; cooler/freezer temperatures 'ranged from 32° to 40°F.'
claims.source: eScholarship/cdlib dissertation PDF (mirror; study of Black women workers)
claims.uncertainty: Reached via an odd mirror URL; underlying dissertation not fully identified in excerpt. Treat figures as provisional pending direct citation.

claims.claim: At Plankington Packing in 1917, Black men earned 43-64 cents/hour while Black women earned about 30 cents/hour for the same work.
claims.evidence: Same dissertation text: 'At the Plankington Packing Company, in 1917, while Black men earned between .43 and .64 per hour, Black women were paid an average of 30¢ per hour for the same work.'
claims.uncertainty: Single-source wage figures via mirror; Plankington was a Milwaukee firm — Chicago-specific wage parity data not located.

entities.name: Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters
entities.description: The labor union organized by Pullman porters in 1925 under A. Philip Randolph — the first Black-led union to win a collective bargaining agreement with a major U.S. corporation (recognized 1937).
entities.chicago_connection: Chicago was a major porter base and organizing center; porters' South Side Chicago community was central to the union.

claims.claim: On August 25, 1925, more than 500 Pullman porters gathered in Harlem to form the BSCP under A. Philip Randolph; the Pullman Company recognized it on August 25, 1937 — the first collective bargaining agreement between a Black-led union and a major U.S. corporation.
claims.evidence: Labor Notes (2025): centennial history of the 1925 founding; Black Enterprise: 'In 1925, A. Philip Randolph organized the Brotherhood of the Sleeping Car Porters (BSCP), but it wasn't until Aug. 25, 1937... that the BSCP was recognized as the official union of the Pullman Porters... The BSCP was the very first African American labor union to sign a collective bargaining agreement with a major U.S. corporation.'
claims.uncertainty: None material; dates corroborated across sources.

entities.name: Chi Tech Collective
entities.description: Chicago South Side community tech organization working on digital inclusion and tech workforce pathways; partnered with the Internet Equity Initiative and Blacks In Technology for a 2024 South Side Tech and Community Expo.
entities.chicago_connection: Chicago, South Side: hosted 'CTC Community Kickback' / Tech and Community Expo (Oct 5, 2024) at The Quarry Event Center (2423 E 75th St, Chicago, IL 60649) serving South Shore, Washington Park, and South Chicago residents.

claims.claim: Chi Tech Collective partnered with the Internet Equity Initiative and Blacks In Technology to host a 2024 Tech and Community Expo aimed at closing the digital divide for South Side residents and small businesses.
claims.evidence: Cook County Digital Inclusion Week 2024 event listing.
claims.uncertainty: AI-specific programming by the collective not documented in sources reviewed; this is digital-inclusion infrastructure adjacent to the AI track, recorded as such.

entities.name: David Blackwell
entities.description: Black mathematician and statistician (1919–2010); Nvidia's 2024 Blackwell GPU architecture — the hardware training modern large language models — was named in his honor, recognizing decision-theory foundations that underpin reinforcement learning.

claims.claim: Nvidia named its 2024 Blackwell GPU architecture (the hardware training large language models) after David Blackwell; co-founders Jensen Huang and Chris Malachowsky chose the name to honor a foundational contributor whose theories on decision-making under uncertainty inform reinforcement learning.
claims.evidence: eurweb coverage of the 2026 documentary on Blackwell and the naming; company statements quoted therein.
claims.uncertainty: The 'direct lineage' framing comes from documentary coverage; Blackwell's work is decision theory/statistics and the connection to modern RL is standard but the popular account may simplify it.

entities.name: Deborah Raji
entities.description: Algorithmic auditing researcher; extended Gender Shades auditing to Amazon Rekognition and works on audit methodology and AI governance. Spoke at UChicago on third-party AI audits.
entities.chicago_connection: Invited speaker at University of Chicago Computer Science on algorithmic auditing and evaluation ('Beyond the Benchmarking Paradigm: Audits & Evaluation in the Age of Artificial Intelligence').

claims.claim: Raji collaborated with Joy Buolamwini at the MIT Media Lab/Algorithmic Justice League auditing commercial facial recognition (Microsoft, Amazon, IBM, Face++, Kairos); their Rekognition study documented gender and racial bias, and public pressure that followed led IBM and Amazon to pause or support regulation of police sales.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia biography with citations; ZDNet interview quotes Raji on Amazon's hostile response to the Rekognition audit.
claims.uncertainty: Causal chain from the audit to corporate decisions also involved parallel activism and 2020 events; the audit and Amazon's response are verified.

claims.claim: Raji's research argues audits alone cannot deliver AI accountability without institutional scaffolding, drawing on audit regimes in finance, environmental, and health regulation (Raji, Xu, Honigsberg & Ho, arXiv 2022).
claims.evidence: AI Weekly summary of the arXiv paper 'Outsider Oversight: Designing a Third Party Audit Ecosystem for AI Governance.'
claims.uncertainty: Paper content confirmed via summary only; full text not reviewed.

entities.name: Deep Learning Indaba
entities.description: Pan-African machine-learning summer school and community (founded 2017) strengthening ML capacity across Africa, with satellite events in ~47 countries.

claims.claim: The Deep Learning Indaba is a summer school strengthening machine learning across Africa, with satellite events in ~47 countries; co-founded by Benjamin Rosman (Wits) and Moustapha Cisse among others.
claims.evidence: Forbes Africa profile of Rosman (Aug 2026) confirms co-founding and 47-country reach; UrbanGeekz confirms Cisse as co-founder.
claims.uncertainty: Full founding team beyond Rosman/Cisse not itemized in sources reviewed.

entities.name: DJ Pierre
entities.description: Chicago DJ/producer whose deliberate misuse of a second-hand TB-303 with Phuture created acid house.
entities.chicago_connection: Chicago acid-house pioneer; bought the TB-303 second-hand in Chicago; gave the track to Ron Hardy at the Music Box

claims.claim: DJ Pierre (Nathaniel Pierre Jones), with Earl 'Spanky' Smith Jr. and Herbert 'Herb J' Jackson, bought a second-hand Roland TB-303 for $40 in 1985; unable to program it as intended, Pierre twisted the resonance/cutoff knobs live over a programmed beat in an hour-long jam; the recording became Phuture's 'Acid Tracks' (Trax, 1987)
claims.evidence: Direct DJ Pierre quotes in DJ Mag 'GAME CHANGERS: PHUTURE ACID TRACKS' and The Fader (2014-08-04)
claims.uncertainty: Purchase year 1985 per DJ Mag 'Perfect Pitch'; release 1987; $40 vs $50 in one later source

claims.claim: They made the track specifically so their idol Ron Hardy could play it at the Music Box; Hardy 'hammered it' and it became known as 'Ron Hardy's Acid Tracks'
claims.evidence: DJ Mag 'DJ PIERRE: PERFECT PITCH' (DJ Pierre interview)

entities.name: Don Cornelius
entities.description: Creator and host of Soul Train; entrepreneur who transformed television's ownership and address. NOT the inventor of television. (Case study: television → Black media.)

entities.name: Dorothy Vaughan
entities.description: Mathematician hired into the West Area Computing unit in 1943 who became NACA's first Black supervisor (1949) and led her unit through the transition from hand computation to electronic programming.

claims.claim: Vaughan was hired by NACA in 1943, assigned to Langley's segregated West Area Computing unit, and in 1949 became the first African-American supervisor at NACA.
claims.evidence: National Geographic: 'Dorothy Vaughan (far left) worked in Langley's segregated West Area computing unit and was promoted to lead the group, making her the first African-American supervisor at the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics.'
claims.source: National Geographic, 'Historic Pictures Show the Hidden Women of the Space Race'
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: Anticipating electronic computers, Vaughan learned FORTRAN — one of the earliest programming languages — and taught it to the women she supervised so they would not become obsolete.
claims.evidence: Secondary accounts (e.g., TikTok/Roberta Dina summary of the history): 'she learned FORTRAN, one of the earliest programming languages, and taught it to the women she supervised. She made sure they did not become obsolete.'
claims.source: Secondary coverage summarizing Shetterly's Hidden Figures
claims.uncertainty: Widely reported from Shetterly's book; not verified against a primary NASA document in this session.

entities.name: E. David Ellington
entities.description: Co-founder (with Malcolm CasSelle) of NetNoir, the 1990s AOL portal for Afrocentric content.

claims.claim: In 1995 Ellington and CasSelle launched NetNoir, an Afrocentric music/sports/education/business portal made available to AOL subscribers
claims.evidence: Futurity (same as for CasSelle); Theory, Culture & Society review of Black Software
claims.uncertainty: same as CasSelle entry

entities.name: Earl 'Spanky' Smith Jr.
entities.description: Phuture member who sourced the TB-303 and programmed the beat behind the acid jam.
entities.chicago_connection: Chicago; bought the TB-303 with DJ Pierre, programmed the beat on 'Acid Tracks'

claims.claim: Earl 'Spanky' Smith Jr. found and bought the second-hand TB-303 (~$40), programmed the beat, and jammed with Pierre and Herb J; Pierre was the one twiddling the 303 knobs
claims.evidence: DJ Pierre's account in DJ Mag 'GAME CHANGERS: PHUTURE ACID TRACKS'

entities.name: Elijah McCoy
entities.description: Trained mechanical engineer who, denied engineering work because of racism, worked as a locomotive fireman and oiler on the Michigan Central Railroad, then invented the automatic steam-engine lubricator (1872).

claims.claim: Elijah McCoy received US 129843 on 1872-07-23 for an improvement in lubricators for steam engines (the automatic lubricator).

myth_audit.claim_as_circulated: Garrett Morgan invented the traffic light.
myth_audit.what_is_documented: Morgan did patent a genuinely novel three-position traffic signal (US 1,475,024, 1923) whose all-directional-stop position was an important safety innovation, and he sold it to GE. He did not invent the traffic light: gas-lit signals date to 1868 London, electric signals to 1912-1914, and his own device used semaphore arms, not lights. The 'invented the yellow light' claim is unsupported.
myth_audit.myth_origin: Mid-century honors (including the reported 1963 US government citation for 'inventing the first traffic signal') plus Black History Month lists that compress 'patented a three-position traffic signal' into 'invented the traffic light.'
myth_audit.patent_or_record: US 1,475,024 (granted Nov 20, 1923); British and Canadian patents also secured; rights sold to General Electric for $40,000.

myth_audit.claim_as_circulated: Garrett Morgan invented the gas mask.
myth_audit.what_is_documented: Morgan was a genuine inventor: he patented a novel smoke hood (US 1,090,936, 1914), won first prize at the Second International Exposition of Safety and Sanitation, and heroically used it in the 1916 Lake Erie tunnel rescue. He did not invent the gas mask — respirators date to the mid-1800s. Claims of WWI military use are unverified.
myth_audit.myth_origin: Conflation of 'breathing device / safety hood' with 'gas mask' in popular Black-history writing, plus genuine heroism of the 1916 tunnel rescue, which made the inflated claim feel earned.

entities.name: Yeshimabeit Milner
entities.description: Founder/CEO of Data for Black Lives (2017), a movement of scientists and activists using data science for racial justice; originator of the 'Abolish Big Data' call for community control of data.

claims.claim: Milner co-founded Data for Black Lives (D4BL) with Lucas Mason-Brown in 2017; it began as a statistical research project at the MIT Media Lab and became a nonprofit using data science to create concrete change in Black people's lives, including COVID-19 racial data compilation and a planned national database of police technologies.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (formation November 2017; founders Milner and Mason-Brown); February 2024 interview with Milner on the movement's aims.
claims.uncertainty: Some sources date founding to August 2016 (initial organizing) vs. November 2017 (formalization). Status of the police-technology database as of 2026 not verified.

claims.claim: Milner's stated position: Big Data functions as an 'ideological regime' determining who decides and who is decided about; 'to abolish Big Data' means putting data in the hands of the people who need it most rather than concentrating it with a few institutions.
claims.evidence: Direct quote from her Het HEM visiting-professor lecture; 2024 interview: 'make data a tool for social change instead of a weapon of political oppression.'
claims.uncertainty: none material — recorded as a stated position, not as an accomplished outcome.
